Music and sound hold deep spiritual significance in Balinese culture, believed to carry healing frequencies that restore balance and inner peace. In Ubud, sound therapy sessions incorporate traditional gamelan music—an intricate ensemble of percussive instruments played in hypnotic rhythms—to guide individuals into meditative states.

Alongside gamelan, Tibetan singing bowls and deep harmonic chanting create vibrational frequencies that clear emotional blockages and soothe the nervous system. Whether experienced in group sound baths or private healing sessions, these therapies offer a unique way to achieve relaxation and heightened awareness.
The Philosophy of Tri Hita Karana: Wellness in Harmony

At the heart of Balinese wellness is the philosophy of Tri Hita Karana, which emphasises harmony between humans, nature, and the spiritual realm. This principle is reflected in every aspect of life in Ubud—from the way temples are designed to the balance between agriculture and conservation.

To truly embrace this philosophy, wellness must extend beyond personal practice—it is about living in a way that respects the environment, honours community, and nurtures the soul. Whether through water purification, yoga, mindful agriculture, or holistic healing, Ubud’s rituals remind us that wellbeing is not an isolated act but an ongoing journey of balance.
Ubud: A Place to Restore, Reconnect, and Embrace Slow Living

Ubud is not just a destination—it is an experience, a sanctuary where wellness is embedded into daily life. From the gentle healing waters of Melukat to the conscious nourishment at Permaculture Bali , every ritual invites you to slow down, reconnect, and embrace Slow Living in its most authentic form.
Long after you’ve left its emerald hills, Ubud stays with you—a quiet whisper in moments of reflection, a reminder of the beauty found in balance.

title: Top 10 Permaculture Techniques to Apply in Tropical Climates
excerpt: The tropics are teeming with life—lush rainforests, vibrant farmlands, and ancient traditions woven into the landscapes. Few places capture this harmony quite like Bali, where permaculture isn’t just a set…

blocks.text: The tropics are teeming with life—lush rainforests, vibrant farmlands, and ancient traditions woven into the landscapes. Few places capture this harmony quite like Bali, where permaculture isn’t just a set of techniques but a philosophy deeply ingrained in daily life. Whether you find yourself wandering through the Tegallalang Rice Paddies or admiring fresh produce at an Organic Farmers Market , you’ll see evidence of regenerative agricultural practices that nourish both the earth and its people.

Permaculture, derived from “permanent agriculture,” is about designing systems that work with nature rather than against it. In tropical climates, where sun and rain reign supreme, these methods are not only beneficial—they are essential. If you’re ready to embrace a more sustainable way of living, whether in Bali or beyond, here are ten powerful permaculture techniques to apply in tropical climates.
1. Agroforestry: The Forest That Feeds

Imagine a forest where every plant serves a purpose—providing food, medicine, or shelter. In Bali, agroforestry is not a novelty; it has been practised for generations. Unlike monoculture farming, where vast plots of land are dedicated to a single crop, agroforestry mimics natural ecosystems, creating a biodiverse haven where plants coexist in harmony.

At permaculture Bali sites, towering coconut trees shade coffee and cacao plants, while spice bushes grow beneath. This multi-layered system has immense benefits: it prevents soil erosion, retains moisture, and improves biodiversity. For travellers interested in sustainability, joining a Bali cultural tour that explores agroforestry farms offers a fascinating glimpse into how nature can provide abundance when nurtured wisely.
2. Water Harvesting: Making Every Drop Count

Tropical regions experience heavy rainfall, yet water management remains a crucial challenge. Permaculturists in Bali have perfected water harvesting techniques to ensure every drop is conserved and used efficiently.

Swales, long trenches dug along contours of the land, capture rainwater and redirect it to gardens. This simple but effective system prevents runoff and ensures soil remains hydrated even during dry spells. Additionally, rainwater collection tanks and pond systems are popular features at permaculture farms, providing water for irrigation and household use.
When visiting a permaculture farm in Bali, you may notice bamboo piping directing water naturally through the landscape—proof that sustainability can be seamlessly integrated into daily life.
3. Composting & Vermiculture: Turning Waste into Gold

A stroll through an Organic Farmers Market reveals a simple truth: the best produce comes from nutrient-rich soil. Composting is the heart of organic farming, transforming food scraps, plant waste, and manure into the ultimate soil conditioner.

Many permaculture farms take composting one step further with vermiculture—using worms to break down organic matter and produce highly fertile soil. Worms digest food scraps and excrete nutrient-rich castings, which improve soil structure and encourage healthy plant growth.

In Bali, this practice aligns beautifully with the island’s commitment to sustainability. Local farms and eco-villages host workshops where visitors can learn how to create their own compost and integrate vermiculture into home gardens.
4. Companion Planting: Nature’s Own Pest Control

Ever noticed basil growing next to tomato plants or marigolds dotting vegetable gardens? This is no accident—it’s companion planting, a method that maximises plant relationships for mutual benefit. By placing compatible plants together, farmers can naturally repel pests, improve soil health, and increase yields. In tropical climates, lemongrass is often planted alongside chilies to deter insects, while banana trees provide shade for delicate herbs.

A Bali cooking class showcasing traditional dishes often highlights the importance of companion planting—many ingredients used in Balinese cuisine are grown together to ensure a flourishing ecosystem.
5. Natural Mulching: Keeping Soil Happy

The tropical sun can be relentless, drying out soil faster than expected. That’s where mulching comes in. Covering the ground with organic materials—such as coconut husks, palm leaves, and rice straw—helps retain moisture, suppress weeds, and regulate soil temperature.

On permaculture farms across Bali, natural mulch is everywhere. It not only keeps soil hydrated but also gradually decomposes, enriching the land with organic matter. The principle is simple: if nature sheds it, let it return to the earth.
6. Hügelkultur: Raised Beds for Abundance

Hügelkultur, a technique originating in Europe, has adapted beautifully to tropical climates. It involves creating raised garden beds filled with layers of logs, branches, compost, and soil. These beds retain moisture exceptionally well and provide a slow-release nutrient source for plants.
Visitors to permaculture Bali farms may find hügelkultur beds growing vibrant vegetables, herbs, and fruit trees—all thriving with minimal need for irrigation.
7. Integrated Animal Systems: A Natural Cycle
Animals play a vital role in regenerative farming. Ducks help control pests in rice paddies, chickens aerate the soil, and goats clear unwanted vegetation.

Many Balinese farms integrate animals into their permaculture systems, ensuring their presence supports a self-sustaining environment. It’s common to see free-roaming chickens scratching at the ground, improving soil aeration as they forage.
8. Renewable Energy: Powering Sustainability

Permaculture extends beyond agriculture—it’s a mindset encompassing all aspects of life, including energy consumption. Bali is home to eco-communities that embrace solar power, biofuel, and biogas digesters.

These technologies drastically reduce reliance on fossil fuels and create self-sufficient energy systems. Many farms have converted organic waste into biogas to fuel cooking and heating, showcasing the potential of renewable solutions.
9. Bamboo Architecture: Sustainable Building
Few materials are as sustainable as bamboo. Used for centuries in tropical regions, bamboo is lightweight, durable, and grows rapidly.

Eco-resorts and permaculture farms in Bali take advantage of this natural resource, crafting everything from homes to furniture using bamboo. The island’s architectural ingenuity proves that sustainability goes beyond farming—it encompasses the way we live and build.
10. Community-Based Permaculture: A Culture of Sharing
Perhaps the most important permaculture principle is community involvement. Sustainability thrives when people work together, sharing knowledge, resources, and traditions.

From Bali cultural tours promoting sustainability to organic farming collectives teaching future generations, Bali showcases the power of shared responsibility. In permaculture, success isn’t measured by individual gains but by how well a system nourishes both the land and its people.

Permaculture in tropical climates is more than a farming technique—it’s a movement of resilience, regeneration, and respect for nature. Whether you’re a traveller embracing Slow Living or a farmer looking to transform the land, these principles offer a roadmap to sustainability.

Bali, with its reverence for nature, stands as a beacon for how permaculture can be seamlessly integrated into daily life. And as you wander through an Organic Farmers Market or marvel at the cascading beauty of the Tegallalang Rice Paddies, you’ll witness firsthand the magic that happens when humans and nature work together.

title: The Allure of Traditional Balinese Architecture: A Blend of Art and Functionality
excerpt: Bali—a name that conjures images of emerald-green landscapes, ornate temples, and an unmistakable air of tranquillity. It is a haven for those seeking not only breathtaking scenery but also a…

blocks.text: Bali—a name that conjures images of emerald-green landscapes, ornate temples, and an unmistakable air of tranquillity. It is a haven for those seeking not only breathtaking scenery but also a deeply rooted cultural experience, one where tradition and modernity harmoniously intertwine. Among its many charms, Bali cultural tours often showcase one of the island’s most exquisite treasures—traditional Balinese architecture. Unlike the imposing skyscrapers of Western cities, Balinese structures are a fascinating interplay of form and function, spirituality and craftsmanship, creating an environment designed as much for the soul as it is for daily life.
The Philosophical Foundations

Balinese architecture is deeply influenced by the island’s Hindu-Buddhist beliefs, particularly the concept of Tri Hita Karana —the principle of balance between humanity, nature, and the divine. This philosophy permeates every aspect of Balinese building design, ensuring that structures are not simply places to dwell, but living entities that interact with their surroundings in a harmonious way.

Whether wandering through a family compound or visiting a temple during Bali cultural tours , one quickly notices the distinctive layout of Balinese spaces. Homes, temples, and public areas are arranged according to the ancient principles of Asta Kosala Kosali , a sacred architectural blueprint dictated by cosmic balance. Structures are positioned to align with cardinal directions, ensuring optimal energy flow and a seamless connection between the physical and the metaphysical.
Open-Air Living: A Distinct Approach to Home Design

A defining characteristic of Balinese architecture is its openness. The traditional Balinese compound consists of multiple pavilions designed for different purposes, rather than a single enclosed structure. This concept allows natural ventilation, promoting airflow that keeps interior spaces cool despite Bali’s tropical climate.

Visitors partaking in a Bali cooking class might find themselves in an authentic Balinese kitchen—an open structure where fragrant spices mingle with the island breeze. Similarly, family temples, or Merajan , sit within each compound, acting as spiritual sanctuaries where daily offerings are made, reinforcing the deep-rooted connection between Balinese households and their deities.
The Role of Nature in Architecture

One cannot discuss Balinese architecture without acknowledging its seamless integration with nature. Whether perched atop cliffs in Uluwatu or nestled amid the famed Tegallalang Rice Paddies , structures are designed to complement rather than compete with their surroundings. The use of locally sourced materials—such as bamboo, teak, and volcanic stone—ensures sustainability, while the incorporation of lush gardens and reflective pools maintains a soothing equilibrium.

Eco-conscious visitors exploring the island often find themselves at an Organic Farmers Market , where they not only experience the richness of Balinese agriculture but also witness how sustainability is interwoven into Balinese lifestyles. The rise of permaculture Bali initiatives further highlights this balance, as architects and farmers alike turn to traditional methods to preserve land fertility and create structures that work in harmony with the environment.
Temples: The Spiritual Heartbeat of Bali

Balinese temples are among the most striking examples of the island’s architectural prowess. Whether adorned with elaborate carvings or set against dramatic backdrops, these spiritual hubs are constructed with meticulous precision. Temples are designed with three distinct sections: Nista Mandala (outer courtyard), Madya Mandala (middle courtyard), and Utama Mandala (innermost sacred space). Each tier represents a level of spiritual purification, leading visitors on a symbolic journey toward enlightenment.

During Bali cultural tours , travellers often have the opportunity to visit iconic temples such as Pura Besakih , the island’s mother temple, or Tirta Empul , where natural springs invite purification rituals. These structures, centuries old yet ever vital, stand as testaments to Bali’s unyielding devotion to preserving tradition.
The Slow Living Influence in Balinese Architecture

For those seeking a retreat from the relentless pace of modernity, the concept of Slow Living finds a perfect embodiment in Balinese architecture. There is an inherent mindfulness to every element of a Balinese home, from the placement of gardens to the arrangement of communal areas. This approach encourages residents and visitors alike to embrace a slower, more intentional rhythm—one where mornings unfold with the scent of frangipani and evenings are spent listening to the soothing hum of gamelan music.

Eco-resorts and wellness retreats across Bali increasingly incorporate these traditional design principles, offering spaces that allow visitors to disconnect from excess and reconnect with essence . The charm lies not only in the visual beauty of these structures but in their ability to enhance a lifestyle steeped in peace and mindfulness.
The Future of Balinese Architecture

As modernization continues to influence the island, there is a growing movement to preserve Bali’s architectural heritage while embracing sustainable innovation. Architects are now merging traditional techniques with eco-friendly solutions , incorporating features such as solar energy, recycled materials, and vertical gardens into new designs. Even as contemporary influences seep into Bali’s urban landscapes, the essence of Balinese architecture remains untouched—rooted in spirituality, environmental consciousness, and artistic mastery.
Closing Thoughts

For those who yearn to experience the true soul of Bali, its architecture serves as a gateway to understanding its cultural depth. The way buildings interact with nature, the way spaces are crafted to encourage spiritual and communal connection, and the way sustainability remains at the heart of design—all of these elements tell a story of a people who live harmoniously with their land. Whether it’s an intricately carved temple or a simple village home, Balinese architecture is far more than aesthetics; it is a living testament to tradition, craftsmanship, and the enduring allure of island life.

If you’re eager to explore this further, perhaps a journey through Bali cultural tours , a hands-on Bali cooking class , or an excursion through the Tegallalang Rice Paddies will provide deeper insights. And for those seeking a lifestyle shift, visiting an Organic Farmers Market or learning about permaculture Bali might just plant the seeds of sustainable inspiration.

title: The Secret to Living Slow in a Fast-Paced World: Lessons from Ubud
excerpt: In a world driven by urgency and constant motion, the art of Slow Living has become more than a luxury—it is a necessity for a balanced and fulfilling life. While…

blocks.text: In a world driven by urgency and constant motion, the art of Slow Living has become more than a luxury—it is a necessity for a balanced and fulfilling life. While the modern world pushes us to chase deadlines and stay perpetually connected, the serene town of Ubud offers an inspiring contrast. Here, time moves differently, shaped by the rhythms of nature and the deep-rooted traditions of the Balinese people. Through meaningful experiences such as Bali cultural tours , exploring Tegallalang Rice Paddies , and immersing in local sustainability efforts like permaculture Bali , Ubud holds the key to a slower, more mindful way of life.
The Philosophy of Slow Living

In Ubud, slowing down does not mean stagnation—it means intentional living. It is about savouring the small moments, finding joy in simplicity, and reconnecting with nature. Whether it’s wandering through the lush Tegallalang Rice Paddies at sunrise, attending a traditional Bali cooking class , or shopping at an Organic Farmers Market , every experience invites one to pause and appreciate the richness of the present moment.

Unlike the rushed urban lifestyle that prioritises productivity over well-being, Ubud embraces a holistic approach to life. The Balinese people have long understood that harmony comes from balance—between work and rest, community and solitude, nature and human innovation.
Lessons from Ubud on Living Slowly
Embracing Local Traditions through Cultural Immersion

One of the most profound ways to slow down in Ubud is by immersing oneself in the town’s rich heritage. Participating in Bali cultural tours allows visitors to gain insight into centuries-old customs, sacred temple rituals, and the deeply spiritual philosophy that influences daily life.

Rather than rushing through tourist attractions, Ubud encourages travellers to engage meaningfully. Observing artisans crafting intricate batik fabrics, witnessing traditional dance performances, or joining a village ceremony offers an intimate glimpse into Balinese culture—an experience that fosters mindfulness and deep appreciation.
Mindful Eating and the Art of Slow Food

Food is more than sustenance in Ubud—it is a form of connection. Taking part in a Bali cooking class is an eye-opening experience, teaching not just the techniques of Balinese cuisine but also the philosophy of preparing food with intention and care.

Many ingredients are sourced from local farms or grown using sustainable methods like permaculture Bali , ensuring that food is in harmony with nature. Cooking is done unhurriedly, with respect for both the ingredients and the process. In learning to prepare dishes such as fragrant satays, fresh sambals, and soothing herbal tonics, participants gain more than culinary skills—they learn to savour each bite with awareness and gratitude.
Connecting With Nature through Sustainable Practices

Nature is the heart of Ubud, and living slowly here means respecting and working alongside the environment. The adoption of permaculture Bali principles ensures sustainable farming and responsible use of resources, preserving the land for generations to come.

Visitors can deepen their understanding of sustainability by visiting an Organic Farmers Market , where locally-grown produce, handmade goods, and eco-friendly products reflect the Balinese commitment to living in balance with the earth. The slow-living philosophy extends beyond relaxation—it is a conscious choice to consume mindfully, support ethical businesses, and reduce environmental impact.
The Tranquillity of the Tegallalang Rice Paddies

Few places embody Slow Living as effortlessly as the breathtaking Tegallalang Rice Paddies . Here, the rhythm of life is dictated by the natural world—the gentle sway of rice stalks in the breeze, the careful steps of farmers tending to their fields, and the golden hues of the afternoon sun over the terraces.

Walking through these iconic landscapes allows one to embrace stillness, to slow the hurried mind, and to experience the beauty of simplicity. Whether sitting quietly to watch the sunrise or engaging in conversations with local farmers, the rice paddies teach that patience, presence, and respect for the land are the keys to a more fulfilling life.
Integrating Ubud’s Lessons into Everyday Life

Living slowly does not require being in Ubud—it is a mindset that can be cultivated anywhere. Incorporating small rituals such as mindful eating, engaging with local communities, practising gratitude, or simply spending time outdoors can create a more harmonious lifestyle.
Cook with intention: Experiment with meals using fresh, local ingredients, and appreciate the process of preparation rather than rushing through it.
Support local artisans and farmers: Choosing ethical and sustainable products helps foster a deeper connection with the community and environment.
Spend time in nature: Whether hiking in the countryside or simply tending to a small garden, reconnecting with the land promotes inner calm and clarity.
Slow down daily routines: Avoid multitasking and take time to savour simple joys—whether it’s a cup of tea, a good book, or a conversation with a loved one.
Conclusion

Ubud is more than a destination—it is a philosophy, a way of life that teaches the beauty of slowing down and living with intention. Through cultural immersion, mindful eating, sustainable practices, and deep connection with nature, one can embrace a life that is not defined by speed but by presence and meaning.

The secret to Slow Living is not found in escaping the fast-paced world but in learning how to move through it with awareness, balance, and grace. Whether among the rice paddies of Ubud or in the midst of daily routines elsewhere, the choice to live slowly remains in our own hands.

title: The Essence of Permaculture: Sustainable Living in the Heart of Ubud
excerpt: There’s something undeniably enchanting about Ubud, Bali. It’s a place where spirituality meets sustainability, where tradition embraces innovation, and where slow living isn’t merely a trend—it’s a way of life….

blocks.text: There’s something undeniably enchanting about Ubud, Bali. It’s a place where spirituality meets sustainability, where tradition embraces innovation, and where slow living isn’t merely a trend—it’s a way of life. From the emerald-green Tegallalang Rice Paddies that cascade down the hillsides to the vibrant stalls of the organic farmers market , Ubud is a paradise for those seeking an authentic and eco-conscious travel experience.

Yet, beyond its serene temples and yoga retreats, a quiet revolution is taking place—one that honours the land and fosters harmony between people and nature. At its core lies permaculture Bali , a philosophy that advocates for sustainable living, ecological balance, and regenerative farming practices. In recent years, this movement has gained momentum, drawing eco-travellers, farmers, and sustainability enthusiasts from around the world. Now, let’s dive deeper into Ubud’s thriving permaculture scene and explore how travellers can actively participate in this green revolution.
The Beauty of Ubud’s Sustainable Farming

Bali is known for its lush landscapes, but few places exemplify sustainable agriculture quite like Ubud. The region’s dedication to environmentally friendly farming is evident, particularly in the famous Tegallalang Rice Paddies , where age-old techniques ensure the land remains fertile for generations. Strolling through these terraced fields, it’s easy to marvel at how local farmers cultivate rice with patience and precision, preserving traditions while embracing modern sustainability practices. Beyond rice cultivation, permaculture Bali takes farming to another level, transforming conventional agriculture into a holistic approach that mimics nature’s ecosystems. Unlike large-scale industrial farms, permaculture gardens in Ubud thrive on biodiversity, soil health, and water conservation. You can witness these principles in action at local permaculture farms, where organic fruits, vegetables, and herbs coexist in a rich, symbiotic environment.
The Role of Permaculture in Ubud’s Eco-Conscious Community

Ubud isn’t just home to picturesque landscapes—it’s also a hub for sustainability advocates who are reshaping the way we interact with the land. Whether through dedicated workshops, farm visits, or engaging in hands-on experiences, travellers can immerse themselves in the world of permaculture and gain a deeper appreciation for ethical farming.

For those keen to learn, Bali cultural tours often include stops at local permaculture farms, where visitors can explore food forests, witness natural composting techniques, and understand the delicate balance between flora and fauna. These tours highlight not only the ecological benefits of permaculture but also the cultural significance behind Bali’s agricultural traditions.
A Feast for the Senses: Farm-to-Table Dining

It’s no surprise that Ubud is home to some of Bali’s best organic dining experiences. Restaurants here take pride in sourcing ingredients locally, with many partnering directly with permaculture farms to ensure a farm-to-table approach. Dining in Ubud isn’t just about flavour—it’s about understanding where food comes from and appreciating the journey from soil to plate.

If you’re eager to get involved, attending a Bali cooking class is a fantastic way to deepen your connection to Balinese cuisine while supporting sustainable food practices. These cooking experiences often begin with a visit to the organic farmers market , where participants hand-pick fresh produce before learning the art of crafting traditional Balinese dishes. Beyond acquiring culinary skills, these classes instil a profound respect for nature and the ingredients it provides.
Markets and Ethical Shopping in Ubud

Speaking of fresh produce, the organic farmers market is a must-visit for anyone seeking ethical, locally sourced goods. Held regularly in Ubud, this market is a vibrant gathering of farmers, artisans, and sustainability enthusiasts who share a common goal—supporting eco-friendly agriculture and conscious consumerism.

Here, you’ll find everything from freshly picked fruits and vegetables to handcrafted soaps, organic teas, and sustainable textiles. It’s a place where travellers can connect with local growers, learn about organic farming techniques, and even pick up eco-conscious souvenirs to take home.
Embracing Slow Living in Ubud

Beyond its commitment to sustainability, Ubud embodies the spirit of slow living , encouraging people to embrace a more mindful, intentional approach to life. The fast-paced demands of modern travel often push tourists to cram as many activities into their itinerary as possible. But here, the philosophy is different—less rushing, more appreciating, and a deeper connection to nature.

Whether it’s unwinding in a jungle retreat, participating in a guided meditation session, or simply wandering through the verdant rice terraces, Ubud inspires travellers to slow down and savour each moment. It’s not just about seeing the sights; it’s about immersing oneself in the rhythms of nature and embracing a lifestyle that prioritises sustainability and well-being.
The Future of Sustainable Tourism in Ubud

As more travellers seek meaningful, eco-conscious experiences, Ubud continues to lead the charge in sustainable tourism. Its dedication to permaculture Bali , organic farming, and ethical consumerism sets a precedent for responsible travel, proving that tourism doesn’t have to come at the expense of the environment.

Ultimately, Ubud’s charm lies in its ability to seamlessly blend tradition with sustainability, luxury with responsibility, and nature with nurture. Whether you’re exploring the Tegallalang Rice Paddies , attending a Bali cooking class , or wandering through the bustling stalls of the organic farmers market , each experience reinforces the importance of mindful, ethical travel.
As the world grapples with environmental challenges, destinations like Ubud offer a refreshing perspective—one where sustainability isn’t just a concept, but a way of life.

Hands-on Balinese Cooking !
During this segment of the tour, you’ll learn how to prepare one or more of the following dishes, depending on seasonal availability :

S ate lilit . Made from either minced beef, chicken, fish, pork, or even turtle meat, it’s mixed with coconut, coconut milk, and a rich blend of vegetables and spices. The satay is then wrapped around bamboo, sugarcane or lemongrass sticks before it’s grilled over charcoal. You can enjoy sate lilit with or without dipping sauce.

Nasi ayam and nasi campur. A plate of  rice comes with different elements of Balinese food, such as a portion of betutu (spiced chicken or duck), mixed vegetables, and a dab of spicy sambal matah (Balinese sauce). Nasi ayam and nasi campur are sometimes served with a bowl of soup. For those who do not want it too spicy, simply ask to reduce the amount of chilli !
This empowering session will equip you with practical skills to start your own Balinese cooking at home.

Bali’s iconic rice paddies are a sight to behold, and a guided walk through these emerald terraces offers insight into the island’s agricultural heritage. blocks.text: Unveil the Wisdom of  Regenerative Permaculture Principles

“Sitting at our back doorsteps, all we need to live a good life lies about us. Sun, wind, people, buildings, stones, sea, birds and plants surround us. Cooperation with all these things brings harmony, opposition to them brings disaster and chaos.” ― Bill Mollison, Introduction to Permaculture
A Guide to Creating Your Own Permaculture Garden in Ubud
A Refreshing Welcome: Organic Fruit Juice

Your adventure begins with a warm Balinese welcome and a refreshing glass of organic fruit juice. Sourced from local farms, this delightful beverage is a taste of the tropical paradise that surrounds you. Sip slowly and let the vibrant flavors awaken your senses.
Explore the Farm: Permaculture can be fun !

Next, take a guided tour of our sprawling organic farm. Throughout the tour Nyoman will educate and amuse you with anecdotes of how Balinese Spirituality is used on a daily basis to improve productivity on the farm. Learn about traditional and modern farming techniques as you stroll through lush vegetable patches, fruit orchards, and herb gardens.
Feed the Animals !

Kids and adults of all ages love to get close up tour beautiful farm animals. Learn the art of composting, turning kitchen scraps and garden waste into nutrient-rich soil.
Create your own organic pesticides and fertilizers using simple, natural ingredients.
This empowering session will equip you with practical skills to start your own sustainable garden at home.

blocks.text: Experience the Essence of Bali: A Journey into Nature and Culture

Embark on a transformative Balinese cultural lifestyle tour that weaves together the beauty of nature, the wisdom of tradition, and the joy of learning sustainable practices. Our curated itinerary offers a 2 hour experience designed to reconnect you with the earth, nourish your body, and inspire your mind.

We will show you how Balinese architecture and spirituality is an integral part of our very traditional lifestyle. A tour of the 4 Temples in Gentong Village, our Rainforest and our Rice Paddies with an explanation of the significance of each to modern daily life.
Refreshing Welcome: Organic Fruit Juice
Balinese Temple architectural & spirituality tour
Food Forest & Farm visit : Feed the Animals !
Rice Paddy & Jungle Walk: compare chemical vs organic techniques
Delicious 100% organic Balinese Meal
INCLUDES :
100% organic meal & organic fruit basket from our food forest !
A Refreshing Welcome: Organic Fruit Juice

Your adventure begins with a warm Balinese welcome and a refreshing glass of organic fruit juice. Sourced from local farms, this delightful beverage is a taste of the tropical paradise that surrounds you. Sip slowly and let the vibrant flavors awaken your senses.
Visit our Temples

Each Balinese village has 3 temples, and every family has their own Family Temple. Wayan your tour guide will introduce to you a day in the life of a Balinese family including in-depth explanations of the religious significance of each temple and the importance of the Ancestors in Balinese culture. Rice Paddy Walk: A Journey Through Tradition

Bali’s iconic rice paddies are a sight to behold, and a guided walk through these emerald terraces offers insight into the island’s agricultural heritage. Discover the Subak irrigation system, a UNESCO-recognized tradition that reflects the Balinese philosophy of harmony between humans, nature, and spirit.
